claim: GGGGCC (G4C2) hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the C9ORF72 gene is the most common genetic cause of frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: GGGGCC (G4C2) hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the C9ORF72 gene is the most common genetic cause of frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011).

claim: C9ORF72 antisense C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs trigger the activation of the PKR/eIF2α-dependent integrated stress response independent of dipeptide repeat proteins.
source: Our study shows that C9ORF72 antisense C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs trigger the activation of the PKR/eIF2α-dependent integrated stress response independent of dipeptide repeat proteins that are produced through repeat-associated non-AUG-initiated translation, leading to global translation inhibition and stress granule formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing PKR/eIF2α activation in cells expressing antisense repeats without DPR proteins (Figures 3, 4).

claim: Reducing PKR levels with either siRNA or morpholinos mitigates integrated stress response and toxicity caused by the antisense C4G2 RNAs in cell lines, primary neurons, and zebrafish.
source: Reducing PKR levels with either siRNA or morpholinos mitigates integrated stress response and toxicity caused by the antisense C4G2 RNAs in cell lines, primary neurons, and zebrafish.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue of toxicity and reduced eIF2α phosphorylation upon PKR knockdown (Figures 3F-G, 4D-G, 7).

claim: Increased phosphorylation of PKR/eIF2α is observed in the frontal cortex of C9ORF72 FTD/ALS patients.
source: Increased phosphorylation of PKR/eIF2α is also observed in the frontal cortex of C9ORF72 FTD/ALS patients.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and immunoblotting data from patient postmortem tissues (Figure 5A-C).

claim: Only antisense C4G2, but not sense G4C2, repeat expanded RNAs robustly activate the PKR/eIF2α pathway and induce aberrant stress granule formation.
source: Finally, only antisense C4G2, but not sense G4C2, repeat expanded RNAs robustly activate the PKR/eIF2α pathway and induce aberrant stress granule formation.
evidence: This is supported by ASO experiments showing that degradation of antisense but not sense RNAs reduces PKR/eIF2α activation (Figure 6).

claim: In 2011, GGGGCC (G4C2) hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the first intron of the chromosome 9 open-reading frame 72 (C9ORF72) gene was identified as the most common genetic cause of frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: In 2011, GGGGCC (G4C2) hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the first intron of the chromosome 9 open-reading frame 72 (C9ORF72) gene was identified as the most common genetic cause of frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), two neurodegenerative diseases that are now believed to belong to a continuous disease spectrum with clinical, pathological, and genetic overlaps (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citations to the original discovery papers.

claim: FTD and ALS are now believed to belong to a continuous disease spectrum with clinical, pathological, and genetic overlaps.
source: In 2011, GGGGCC (G4C2) hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the first intron of the chromosome 9 open-reading frame 72 (C9ORF72) gene was identified as the most common genetic cause of frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), two neurodegenerative diseases that are now believed to belong to a continuous disease spectrum with clinical, pathological, and genetic overlaps (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature establishing the relationship between FTD and ALS.

claim: In normal populations, the G4C2 repeat size is between 2 and 30.
source: In normal populations, the G4C2 repeat size is between 2 and 30, whereas it expands to hundreds or thousands in FTD/ALS patients (referred to hereafter as C9FTD/ALS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about normal repeat sizes in the general population.

claim: In FTD/ALS patients, the G4C2 repeat expands to hundreds or thousands.
source: In normal populations, the G4C2 repeat size is between 2 and 30, whereas it expands to hundreds or thousands in FTD/ALS patients (referred to hereafter as C9FTD/ALS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pathological repeat expansions in C9ORF72 patients.

claim: Expanded G4C2 repeats inhibit C9ORF72 mRNA transcription, leading to haploinsufficiency of the C9ORF72 protein.
source: First, expanded G4C2 repeats inhibit C9ORF72 mRNA transcription, leading to haploinsufficiency of the C9ORF72 protein (Braems et al., 2020; Gijselinck et al., 2012; van Blitterswijk et al., 2015);
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing reduced C9ORF72 expression in patients.

claim: C9ORF72 repeats are bidirectionally transcribed into sense G4C2 and antisense CCCCGG (C4G2) RNAs.
source: second, C9ORF72 repeats are bidirectionally transcribed into sense G4C2 and antisense CCCCGG (C4G2) RNAs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bidirectional transcription of C9ORF72 repeats.

claim: Translating from sense G4C2 RNAs produces GA (glycine-alanine), GP (glycine-proline), and GR (glycine-arginine) DPR proteins.
source: More specifically, translating from sense G4C2 RNAs produces GA (glycine-alanine), GP (glycine-proline), and GR (glycine-arginine) DPR proteins, and translating from antisense C4G2 RNAs produces GP (glycine-proline), PA (proline-alanine), and PR (proline-arginine) DPR proteins (Ash et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ash et al., 2013 describing RAN translation products.

claim: Translating from antisense C4G2 RNAs produces GP (glycine-proline), PA (proline-alanine), and PR (proline-arginine) DPR proteins.
source: More specifically, translating from sense G4C2 RNAs produces GA (glycine-alanine), GP (glycine-proline), and GR (glycine-arginine) DPR proteins, and translating from antisense C4G2 RNAs produces GP (glycine-proline), PA (proline-alanine), and PR (proline-arginine) DPR proteins (Ash et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ash et al., 2013 describing RAN translation products.

claim: There is evidence of chimeric DPR proteins in both model systems and patients.
source: In addition to these pure dimeric DPR proteins, there is also evidence of chimeric DPR proteins in both model systems and patients (Gao et al., 2017; McEachin et al., 2020a; Tabet et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies reporting chimeric DPR proteins.

claim: Reducing C9ORF72 in zebrafish or Caenorhabditis elegans can cause motor deficits.
source: Although reducing C9ORF72 in zebrafish or Caenorhabditis elegans can cause motor deficits (Swinnen et al., 2018; Therrien et al., 2013), reduced or even complete deletion of C9ORF72 in mice does not lead to FTD/ALS-like abnormalities, suggesting that loss of C9ORF72 is not the main disease driver (Atanasio et al., 2016; Burberry et al., 2016; Koppers et al., 2015; O'Rourke et al., 2016; Sudria-Lopez et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2016; Ugolino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in zebrafish and C. elegans models.

claim: Reduced or even complete deletion of C9ORF72 in mice does not lead to FTD/ALS-like abnormalities.
source: Although reducing C9ORF72 in zebrafish or Caenorhabditis elegans can cause motor deficits (Swinnen et al., 2018; Therrien et al., 2013), reduced or even complete deletion of C9ORF72 in mice does not lead to FTD/ALS-like abnormalities, suggesting that loss of C9ORF72 is not the main disease driver (Atanasio et al., 2016; Burberry et al., 2016; Koppers et al., 2015; O'Rourke et al., 2016; Sudria-Lopez et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2016; Ugolino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to mouse knockout studies.

claim: Loss of C9ORF72 is not the main disease driver.
source: Although reducing C9ORF72 in zebrafish or Caenorhabditis elegans can cause motor deficits (Swinnen et al., 2018; Therrien et al., 2013), reduced or even complete deletion of C9ORF72 in mice does not lead to FTD/ALS-like abnormalities, suggesting that loss of C9ORF72 is not the main disease driver (Atanasio et al., 2016; Burberry et al., 2016; Koppers et al., 2015; O'Rourke et al., 2016; Sudria-Lopez et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2016; Ugolino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited mouse knockout studies showing no FTD/ALS phenotype.

claim: No missense or truncation mutations in C9ORF72 are yet found in FTD/ALS patients.
source: Supporting this, no missense or truncation mutations in C9ORF72 are yet found in FTD/ALS patients (Harms et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harms et al., 2013.

claim: Gain of toxicity from the repeat expanded RNAs plays a central role in disease pathogenesis.
source: On the other hand, several lines of studies, by expressing either G4C2 repeats (Chew et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2016) or individual codon-optimized, ATG-driven DPR proteins (Choi et al., 2019; Mizielinska et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019), support that gain of toxicity from the repeat expanded RNAs plays a central role in disease pathogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing toxicity from repeat RNAs and DPR proteins.

claim: Loss of C9ORF72 can exacerbate toxicity from the repeat expanded RNAs.
source: Finally, loss of C9ORF72, which plays a role in autophagy/lysosomal functions, can exacerbate toxicity from the repeat expanded RNAs (Boivin et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing interaction between C9ORF72 loss and repeat RNA toxicity.

claim: C9ORF72 plays a role in autophagy/lysosomal functions.
source: Finally, loss of C9ORF72, which plays a role in autophagy/lysosomal functions, can exacerbate toxicity from the repeat expanded RNAs (Boivin et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C9ORF72 function.

claim: Several RBPs have been suggested to interact with G4C2 or C4G2 repeat RNAs and to co-localize with RNA foci.
source: Several RBPs have been suggested to interact with G4C2 or C4G2 repeat RNAs and to co-localize with RNA foci (Celona et al., 2017; Conlon et al., 2016; Donnelly et al., 2013; Haeusler et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Mori et al., 2013; Sareen et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies identifying RBP interactions with repeat RNAs.

claim: Strong evidence supporting that loss of any proposed RBPs drives C9FTD/ALS is lacking.
source: However, strong evidence supporting that loss of any proposed RBPs drives C9FTD/ALS is lacking.
evidence: This is an assessment of the literature indicating insufficient evidence for RBP sequestration as a primary mechanism.

claim: Ectopic expression of individual DPR proteins, especially GR and PR, causes toxicity in various model systems.
source: In contrast, ectopic expression of individual DPR proteins, especially GR and PR, causes toxicity in various model systems (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Choi et al., 2019; Freibaum et al., 2015; Hao et al., 2019; Kanekura et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016; May et al., 2014; Mizielinska et al., 2014; Schludi et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2015; Wen et al., 2014; Yamakawa et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2014; Zu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to studies showing DPR protein toxicity.

claim: Neither sense or antisense repeat expanded RNAs are toxic in Drosophila when DPR protein production is prevented.
source: To determine the relative contributions of RNA foci- and DPR protein-mediated toxicity, two studies employed interrupted repeats with stop codons in all reading frames to prevent DPR protein production and concluded that neither sense or antisense repeat expanded RNAs are toxic in Drosophila (Moens et al., 2018; Tran et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Drosophila studies using interrupted repeats.

claim: Both sense and antisense repeat expanded RNAs can cause motor axonopathy in zebrafish independent of DPR proteins.
source: This was challenged by another study showing both sense and antisense repeat expanded RNAs can cause motor axonopathy in zebrafish independent of DPR proteins (Swinnen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a zebrafish study showing RNA-mediated toxicity.

claim: ASOs to selectively degrade sense G4C2 repeat expanded RNAs mitigate toxicity from C9ORF72 repeat expansions in transgenic mice expressing G4C2 repeats.
source: These sense strand-specific ASOs not only mitigate toxicity from C9ORF72 repeat expansions in both transgenic mice expressing G4C2 repeats (Jiang et al., 2016) and patient IPSC-derived neurons (Donnelly et al., 2013), but also reverse downstream cellular and molecular alterations such as nucleocytoplasmic transport deficits (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2016 showing ASO efficacy in mice.

claim: ASOs to selectively degrade sense G4C2 repeat expanded RNAs mitigate toxicity in patient IPSC-derived neurons.
source: These sense strand-specific ASOs not only mitigate toxicity from C9ORF72 repeat expansions in both transgenic mice expressing G4C2 repeats (Jiang et al., 2016) and patient IPSC-derived neurons (Donnelly et al., 2013), but also reverse downstream cellular and molecular alterations such as nucleocytoplasmic transport deficits (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Donnelly et al., 2013 showing ASO efficacy in patient neurons.

claim: Sense strand-specific ASOs reverse nucleocytoplasmic transport deficits.
source: These sense strand-specific ASOs not only mitigate toxicity from C9ORF72 repeat expansions in both transgenic mice expressing G4C2 repeats (Jiang et al., 2016) and patient IPSC-derived neurons (Donnelly et al., 2013), but also reverse downstream cellular and molecular alterations such as nucleocytoplasmic transport deficits (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: PR or its aggregates are rare in postmortem tissues.
source: Although PR translated from the antisense strand is extremely toxic in model systems, PR or its aggregates are rare in postmortem tissues.
evidence: This is an observation about the pathology of C9ORF72 patients.

claim: Antisense RNA transcripts are hard to detect.
source: Antisense RNA transcripts are also hard to detect.
evidence: This is an observation about the technical difficulty of detecting antisense transcripts.

claim: Antisense RNA foci are as abundant as sense RNA foci in multiple brain regions.
source: Surprisingly, several studies showed that antisense RNA foci are as abundant as sense RNA foci in multiple brain regions (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2017; Mizielinska et al., 2013; Vatsavayai et al., 2019), raising a possibility that antisense C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs also contribute to C9FTD/ALS (McEachin et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuropathological studies.

claim: Antisense C9ORF72 C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs are neurotoxic independent of RAN translated DPR proteins.
source: In this study, we show that antisense C9ORF72 C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs are neurotoxic independent of RAN translated DPR proteins.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Antisense C4G2, but not sense G4C2, repeat expanded RNAs activate PKR/eIF2α-dependent integrated stress response.
source: Antisense C4G2, but not sense G4C2, repeat expanded RNAs activate PKR/eIF2α-dependent integrated stress response, leading to global protein synthesis inhibition and stress granules formation.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The phosphorylation of PKR/eIF2α is significantly increased in C9FTD/ALS patients.
source: Moreover, the phosphorylation of PKR/eIF2α is significantly increased in C9FTD/ALS patients, suggesting that antisense C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs contribute to disease pathogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by data from patient postmortem tissues in Figure 5.

claim: HEK293T cells expressing in_(C4G2)75 show an abundant accumulation of antisense RNA foci.
source: When expressed in HEK293T cells, we detected an abundant accumulation of antisense RNA foci, but not in control cells expressing 2 C4G2 repeats (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1B with RNA FISH data.

claim: GP, PR, and PA DPR proteins are produced only in cells expressing in_(C4G2)75 but not 2 repeats.
source: Using antibodies against individual DPR proteins RAN translated from C4G2 expanded repeat RNAs or the protein tags in frame, we also observed production of GP, PR, and PA DPR proteins only in cells expressing in_(C4G2)75 but not 2 repeats (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence and western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Antisense RNA foci and DPR proteins are observed in mouse primary cortical neurons expressing in_(C4G2)75.
source: Antisense RNA foci and DPR proteins were also observed in mouse primary cortical neurons expressing in_(C4G2)75, but not in neurons expressing 2 repeats (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neurons expressing in_(C4G2)75 die much faster than those expressing control 2 repeats.
source: Neurons expressing in_(C4G2)75 die much faster than those expressing control 2 repeats, suggesting that C9ORF72 antisense C4G2 expanded repeats are neurotoxic (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown by longitudinal microscopy survival data in Figure 1C.

claim: HEK293T cells expressing in_(C4G2)75 show a significant increase in the level of phosphorylated PKR compared to cells expressing 2 repeats.
source: HEK293T cells expressing in_(C4G2)75 show a significant increase in the level of phosphorylated PKR compared to cells expressing 2 repeats, while the total level of PKR remains unchanged (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The total level of PKR remains unchanged in cells expressing in_(C4G2)75.
source: HEK293T cells expressing in_(C4G2)75 show a significant increase in the level of phosphorylated PKR compared to cells expressing 2 repeats, while the total level of PKR remains unchanged (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 1D and E.

claim: PKR is one of four kinases that are activated during the integrated stress response (ISR).
source: PKR is one of four kinases that are activated during the integrated stress response (ISR), an evolutionarily conserved stress signaling pathway that adjusts cellular biosynthetic capacity according to need (Martinez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ISR pathway, supported by citation.

claim: The four ISR kinases include PKR, PKR-like ER kinase (PERK), heme-regulated eIF2α kinase (HRI), and general control non-derepressible 2 (GCN2).
source: The four ISR kinases, including PKR, PKR-like ER kinase (PERK), heme-regulated eIF2α kinase (HRI), and general control non-derepressible 2 (GCN2), respond to distinct environmental and physiological stresses by phosphorylating the eukaryotic translation initiation factor eIF2α to cause a temporary shutdown of global protein synthesis and upregulation of specific stress-responsive genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ISR kinases.

claim: ISR kinases respond to distinct environmental and physiological stresses by phosphorylating eIF2α to cause a temporary shutdown of global protein synthesis and upregulation of specific stress-responsive genes.
source: The four ISR kinases, including PKR, PKR-like ER kinase (PERK), heme-regulated eIF2α kinase (HRI), and general control non-derepressible 2 (GCN2), respond to distinct environmental and physiological stresses by phosphorylating the eukaryotic translation initiation factor eIF2α to cause a temporary shutdown of global protein synthesis and upregulation of specific stress-responsive genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ISR function.

claim: in_(C4G2)75 significantly increases the phosphorylation of eIF2α without affecting its total level.
source: Accompanying PKR activation, in_(C4G2)75 significantly increases the phosphorylation of eIF2α without affecting its total level (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 1F and G.

claim: in_(C4G2)75 activates eIF2α mainly by the phosphorylation of PKR as other ISR kinases such as PERK phosphorylation are not altered.
source: in_(C4G2)75 activates eIF2α mainly by the phosphorylation of PKR as other ISR kinases such as PERK phosphorylation are not altered (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing no change in PERK phosphorylation.

claim: Overexpressing wild type PKR further increases the phosphorylation of eIF2α induced by in_(C4G2)75.
source: Consistent with this, overexpressing wild type (WT) PKR further increases the phosphorylation of eIF2α induced by in_(C4G2)75, whereas treatment with a specific PKR inhibitor C16 reduces the phosphorylation of both PKR and eIF2α to a level comparable to that of cells expressing 2 repeats (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Treatment with a specific PKR inhibitor C16 reduces the phosphorylation of both PKR and eIF2α to a level comparable to that of cells expressing 2 repeats.
source: Consistent with this, overexpressing wild type (WT) PKR further increases the phosphorylation of eIF2α induced by in_(C4G2)75, whereas treatment with a specific PKR inhibitor C16 reduces the phosphorylation of both PKR and eIF2α to a level comparable to that of cells expressing 2 repeats (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 1H and I.

claim: SH-SY5Y cells expressing in_(C4G2)75 show activation of PKR and eIF2α by the antisense C4G2 expanded repeats.
source: We further expressed in_(C4G2)75 in a neuronal cell line SH-SY5Y that is commonly used to study neurodegeneration and observed similar activation of PKR and eIF2α by the antisense C4G2 expanded repeats (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: HEK293T cells expressing in_(C4G2)75 show a significantly reduced amount of incorporated puromycin compared to those expressing 2 repeats.
source: HEK293T cells expressing in_(C4G2)75 show a significantly reduced amount of incorporated puromycin compared to those expressing 2 repeats (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by puromycin incorporation assay in Figure 2A.

claim: Neurons expressing 75 antisense C4G2 repeats have a robust global translation inhibition.
source: Similarly, neurons expressing 75 antisense C4G2 repeats, as identified by GP DPR protein accumulation, have a robust global translation inhibition (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is shown by puromycin incorporation data in primary neurons in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Approximately 32% of cells expressing in_(C4G2)75 show G3BP1-positive stress granules.
source: Approximately 32% of cells expressing in_(C4G2)75, identified by the presence of antisense RNA foci, show G3BP1-positive stress granules, and ~55% of foci-positive cells stain for FMRP, another commonly used marker for stress granules (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Approximately 55% of foci-positive cells stain for FMRP.
source: Approximately 32% of cells expressing in_(C4G2)75, identified by the presence of antisense RNA foci, show G3BP1-positive stress granules, and ~55% of foci-positive cells stain for FMRP, another commonly used marker for stress granules (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Neither PR50, PA50, nor GP80 activates the phosphorylation of eIF2α.
source: We first expressed individual codon-optimized, ATG-driven DPR proteins. Neither PR50, PA50, nor GP80 activates the phosphorylation of eIF2α, suggesting that the activation of the PKR/eIF2α pathway by C9ORF72 antisense C4G2 expanded repeats is unlikely due to the DPR proteins produced from RAN translation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The activation of the PKR/eIF2α pathway by C9ORF72 antisense C4G2 expanded repeats is unlikely due to the DPR proteins produced from RAN translation.
source: We first expressed individual codon-optimized, ATG-driven DPR proteins. Neither PR50, PA50, nor GP80 activates the phosphorylation of eIF2α, suggesting that the activation of the PKR/eIF2α pathway by C9ORF72 antisense C4G2 expanded repeats is unlikely due to the DPR proteins produced from RAN translation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing individual DPR proteins do not activate PKR/eIF2α.

claim: C9ORF72 sense G4C2 repeat expanded RNAs initiate RAN translation at a near-cognate CUG codon in the intronic region 24 nucleotides upstream of the repeat sequence.
source: First, recent studies have shown that C9ORF72 sense G4C2 repeat expanded RNAs initiate RAN translation at a near-cognate CUG codon in the intronic region 24 nucleotides upstream of the repeat sequence (Green et al., 2017; Tabet et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying the RAN translation initiation site.

claim: Cells expressing (C4G2)75 do not accumulate any detectable GP, PA, or PR DPR proteins.
source: Supporting our hypothesis, cells expressing (C4G2)75 do not accumulate any detectable GP, PA, or PR DPR proteins, which is strikingly different compared to those expressing in_(C4G2)75 with the 450 bp human intronic sequence (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 3B.

claim: The levels of RNA transcripts and antisense foci are comparable between (C4G2)75 and in_(C4G2)75.
source: The reduced/abolished DPR proteins by (C4G2)75 are not due to altered RNA expressions since the levels of RNA transcripts and antisense foci are comparable to those of in_(C4G2)75 (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by qPCR and RNA FISH data in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No detectable antisense DPR proteins are observed in cells expressing (C4G2)108RO.
source: As expected, no detectable antisense DPR proteins are observed in cells expressing (C4G2)108RO, despite an abundant accumulation of antisense foci (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is shown by western blot and RNA FISH data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Expression of either (C4G2)75 or (C4G2)108RO leads to the robust activation of PKR and eIF2α at a comparable level as seen for in_(C4G2)75.
source: Interestingly, expression of either (C4G2)75 or (C4G2)108RO leads to the robust activation of PKR and eIF2α at a comparable level as seen for in_(C4G2)75 (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Nearly 100% of (C4G2)108RO-expressing neurons show the presence of antisense foci.
source: We observed the presence of antisense foci in nearly 100% of (C4G2)108RO-expressing neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) together with increased levels of phosphorylated eIF2α (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is shown by RNA FISH data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: (C4G2)108RO-expressing neurons show increased levels of phosphorylated eIF2α.
source: We observed the presence of antisense foci in nearly 100% of (C4G2)108RO-expressing neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) together with increased levels of phosphorylated eIF2α (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Reducing PKR in (C4G2)108RO-expressing neurons mitigates the elevated levels of phosphorylated eIF2α.
source: Since the available commercial antibodies against mouse phosphorylated PKR do not work in our hands, we designed siRNAs targeting mouse PKR. Reducing PKR in (C4G2)108RO-expressing neurons mitigates the elevated levels of phosphorylated eIF2α (Figure 3F and G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence and western blot data in Figure 3F and G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: FMRP and G3BP1 rapidly assemble into stress granules in cells expressing (C4G2)108RO.
source: We found that FMRP and G3BP1 are mainly diffused in the cytoplasm of cells expressing 2 C4G2 repeats as expected, but they rapidly assemble into stress granules in cells expressing (C4G2)108RO (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Antisense C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs themselves can trigger stress granule formation in the absence of DPR proteins.
source: These data suggest that antisense C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs themselves can trigger stress granule formation in the absence of DPR proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing stress granules in (C4G2)108RO-expressing cells without DPR proteins.

claim: siRNAs targeting PKR reduce its protein level by 80% compared to control siRNAs.
source: siRNAs targeting PKR reduce its protein level by 80% compared to control siRNAs (Figure 4D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 4D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The phosphorylation of eIF2α by (C4G2)108RO is almost inhibited when PKR is knocked down.
source: Consequently, the phosphorylation of eIF2α by (C4G2)108RO is almost inhibited (Figure 4D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H) and the percentage of foci-positive cells with stress granules is significantly reduced (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 4D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The percentage of foci-positive cells with stress granules is significantly reduced when PKR is knocked down.
source: Consequently, the phosphorylation of eIF2α by (C4G2)108RO is almost inhibited (Figure 4D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H) and the percentage of foci-positive cells with stress granules is significantly reduced (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 4E and F.

claim: A slight but significant increase in the global protein synthesis is observed when PKR is knocked down in (C4G2)108RO-expressing cells.
source: Furthermore, a slight but significant increase in the global protein synthesis is also observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is shown by puromycin incorporation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Neurons expressing (C4G2)108RO show a significant decrease in survival compared to control neurons expressing 2 repeats.
source: Neurons expressing (C4G2)108RO show a significant decrease in survival compared to control neurons expressing 2 repeats (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown by longitudinal microscopy survival data in Figure 4G.

claim: Knockdown of PKR partially rescues the (C4G2)108RO-mediated toxicity.
source: Importantly, knockdown of PKR partially rescues the (C4G2)108RO-mediated toxicity (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown by longitudinal microscopy survival data in Figure 4G.

claim: The level of phosphorylated PKR is increased in the frontal cortex, especially in the large pyramidal neurons, of patients carrying C9ORF72 repeat expansions compared to age-matched non-disease controls.
source: Immunohistochemistry staining showed that the level of phosphorylated PKR is increased in the frontal cortex, especially in the large pyramidal neurons, of patients carrying C9ORF72 repeat expansions compared to age-matched non-disease controls (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5A.

claim: Two recent studies show increased PKR phosphorylation in C9ORF72 patients.
source: This data is consistent with two recent studies showing increased PKR phosphorylation in C9ORF72 patients (Rodriguez et al., 2021; Zu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rodriguez et al., 2021 and Zu et al., 2020.

claim: The level of phosphorylated eIF2α after normalizing to the total eIF2α level is significantly increased in C9FTD/ALS patients.
source: In addition, the level of phosphorylated eIF2α after normalizing to the total eIF2α level is also significantly increased, despite the heterogeneity of eIF2α protein levels in patients (Figure 5B and C, Table 1).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The PKR/eIF2α pathway is activated in C9FTD/ALS patients.
source: These results suggest that the PKR/eIF2α pathway is activated in C9FTD/ALS patients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased phosphorylation of PKR and eIF2α in patient tissues.

claim: No differences in the levels of either phosphorylated PKR or phosphorylated eIF2α are observed in 38-day-old C9ORF72 patient-derived motor neurons compared to isogenic controls.
source: However, we did not observe any differences in the levels of either phosphorylated PKR or phosphorylated eIF2α of 38-day-old neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that PKR/ eIF2α-dependent ISR pathway possibly gets activated in C9ORF72 patients in a later stage of disease pathogenesis.
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: PKR/eIF2α-dependent ISR pathway possibly gets activated in C9ORF72 patients in a later stage of disease pathogenesis.
source: However, we did not observe any differences in the levels of either phosphorylated PKR or phosphorylated eIF2α of 38-day-old neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that PKR/ eIF2α-dependent ISR pathway possibly gets activated in C9ORF72 patients in a later stage of disease pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of PKR/eIF2α activation in young iPSC-derived neurons.

claim: Expression of sense (G4C2)75 in HEK293T cells significantly increases phosphorylation of both PKR and eIF2α.
source: Consistent with the earlier findings by Zu et al., expression of sense (G4C2)75 in HEK293T cells significantly increases phosphorylation of both PKR and eIF2α (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Abundant accumulation of both sense and antisense RNA foci is detected in cells expressing sense (G4C2)75.
source: However, we detected abundant accumulation of both sense and antisense RNA foci in cells expressing sense (G4C2)75 but not in those expressing 2 repeats (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by RNA FISH data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Accumulation of sense foci is detected in cells expressing antisense (C4G2) expanded repeats.
source: Interestingly, we also detected accumulation of sense foci in cells expressing antisense (C4G2) expanded repeats in such model system (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by RNA FISH data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ASOs targeting sense G4C2 repeat expanded RNAs significantly reduce the accumulation of sense RNA foci but have little effect on antisense RNA foci.
source: As expected, ASOs targeting sense G4C2 repeat expanded RNAs significantly reduce the accumulation of sense RNA foci but have little effect on antisense RNA foci (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by RNA FISH data in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Reducing sense G4C2 RNA transcripts/foci does not alter the activation of PKR/eIF2α by (G4C2)75.
source: However, reducing sense G4C2 RNA transcripts/foci does not alter the activation of PKR/eIF2α by (G4C2)75 (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Both ASO1 and ASO2 targeting antisense C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs significantly reduce the abundance of antisense RNA foci without affecting sense RNA foci.
source: We next designed two ASOs specifically targeting antisense repeat RNAs. Both ASO1 and ASO2 targeting antisense C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs significantly reduce the abundance of antisense RNA foci without affecting sense RNA foci (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown by RNA FISH data in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both ASOs targeting antisense RNAs significantly inhibit the activation of PKR and eIF2α by (G4C2)75.
source: Consequently, both ASOs significantly inhibit the activation of PKR and eIF2α by (G4C2)75 (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Expression of sense (G4C2)108RO significantly increases the phosphorylation of PKR and eIF2α.
source: We further obtained an interrupted sense (G4C2)108RO construct that has the similar repeat size as the antisense (C4G2)108RO (Moens et al., 2018). Expression of sense (G4C2)108RO also significantly increases the phosphorylation of PKR and eIF2α, which is mitigated by ASOs targeting antisense RNAs, but not sense RNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The phosphorylation of PKR and eIF2α by sense (G4C2)108RO is mitigated by ASOs targeting antisense RNAs, but not sense RNAs.
source: We further obtained an interrupted sense (G4C2)108RO construct that has the similar repeat size as the antisense (C4G2)108RO (Moens et al., 2018). Expression of sense (G4C2)108RO also significantly increases the phosphorylation of PKR and eIF2α, which is mitigated by ASOs targeting antisense RNAs, but not sense RNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown by western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: A significant increase in the accumulation of FMRP and G3BP1 granules is observed in (G4C2)75 repeats expressing cells compared to those expressing the control 2 repeats.
source: We observed a significant increase in the accumulation of FMRP and G3BP1 granules in (G4C2)75 repeats expressing cells compared to those expressing the control 2 repeats.
evidence: This is an observation about stress granule formation in sense repeat-expressing cells.

claim: Aberrant accumulation of stress granules is drastically reduced after treatment with ASOs targeting the antisense G4C2 repeat RNAs.
source: Interestingly, such aberrant accumulation of stress granules is drastically reduced after treatment with ASOs targeting the antisense G4C2 repeat RNAs (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Co-injection of antisense (C4G2)70 RNAs with eif2ak2 SB-MO significantly mitigates the abnormalities of axonal length and branching compared to zebrafish injected with (C4G2)70 RNAs and a control morpholino.
source: Co-injection of antisense (C4G2)70 RNAs with eif2ak2 SB-MO significantly mitigates the abnormalities of axonal length and branching compared to zebrafish injected with (C4G2)70 RNAs and a control morpholino (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is shown by zebrafish motor axon phenotyping data in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Eif2ak2 reduction with a translation-blocking morpholino increases axonal length and significantly ameliorates the abnormal branching phenotype caused by antisense (C4G2)70 RNAs.
source: Consistent with this observation, Eif2ak2 reduction with a translation-blocking morpholino increases axonal length (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C) and significantly ameliorates the abnormal branching phenotype caused by antisense (C4G2)70 RNAs.
evidence: This is shown by zebrafish motor axon phenotyping data in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: No protective effects are observed when co-injecting sense (G4C2)70 RNAs with eif2ak2 SB-MO.
source: On the other hand, no protective effects were observed when co-injecting sense (G4C2)70 RNAs with eif2ak2 SB-MO (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is shown by zebrafish motor axon phenotyping data in Figure 7E and F.

claim: PKR is an important player contributing to toxicity induced by antisense C4G2 but not sense G4C2 repeat expanded RNAs.
source: Overall, these data indicate that PKR is an important player contributing to toxicity induced by antisense C4G2 but not sense G4C2 repeat expanded RNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the zebrafish rescue experiments showing PKR knockdown rescues antisense but not sense RNA toxicity.

claim: Repeat expanded RNAs, including CAG, CUG, CCUG, CAGG, and G4C2, have been shown to activate the double-stranded RNA-dependent protein kinase (PKR).
source: More than 50 neurological diseases are genetically associated with microsatellite repeat expansions. Repeat expanded RNAs, including CAG, CUG, CCUG, CAGG, and G4C2, have been shown to activate the double-stranded RNA-dependent protein kinase (PKR) (Handa et al., 2003; Tian et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing PKR activation by various repeat RNAs.

claim: Antisense C4G2 DNAs form i-motifs consisting of two parallel duplexes in a head to tail orientation as well as protonated hairpins under near-physiological conditions.
source: It has been shown that antisense C4G2 DNAs form i-motifs consisting of two parallel duplexes in a head to tail orientation as well as protonated hairpins under near-physiological conditions, thus posing a possibility of direct activation of PKR by antisense RNA (Kovanda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kovanda et al., 2015.

claim: Sense G4C2 RNAs exist in an equilibrium between two folded states, hairpin and G-quadruplex.
source: In contrast, sense G4C2 RNAs exist in an equilibrium between two folded states, hairpin and G-quadruplex (Wang et al., 2019), and tend to form more stable unimolecular and multimolecular G-quadruplexes (Fratta et al., 2012; Reddy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of G4C2 RNAs.

claim: Sense G4C2 RNAs tend to form more stable unimolecular and multimolecular G-quadruplexes.
source: In contrast, sense G4C2 RNAs exist in an equilibrium between two folded states, hairpin and G-quadruplex (Wang et al., 2019), and tend to form more stable unimolecular and multimolecular G-quadruplexes (Fratta et al., 2012; Reddy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of G4C2 RNAs.

claim: dsRNAs, derived at least in part from G4C2 repeats, colocalize with phosphorylated TDP-43 in the cerebellum and frontal cortex of C9FTD/ALS patients.
source: Indeed, Rodriguez et al., 2021 showed dsRNAs, derived at least in part from G4C2 repeats, colocalize with phosphorylated TDP-43 in the cerebellum and frontal cortex of C9FTD/ALS patients.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rodriguez et al., 2021.

claim: Transcripts from multiple classes of repetitive elements are significantly elevated in C9ORF72 patients.
source: In C9ORF72 patients, transcripts from multiple classes of repetitive elements are significantly elevated (Prudencio et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prudencio et al., 2017.

claim: Chronic stress during aging or under pathological conditions leads to altered stress granule dynamics and persistent stress granules.
source: Stress granules are dynamic structures that form and disperse rapidly with acute stress. However, chronic stress during aging or under pathological conditions leads to altered stress granule dynamics and persistent stress granules, which have been implicated in the aggregation of RBPs such as TDP-43 and contribute to the pathogenesis of FTD and ALS (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about stress granule pathology, supported by citation.

claim: Persistent stress granules have been implicated in the aggregation of RBPs such as TDP-43 and contribute to the pathogenesis of FTD and ALS.
source: Stress granules are dynamic structures that form and disperse rapidly with acute stress. However, chronic stress during aging or under pathological conditions leads to altered stress granule dynamics and persistent stress granules, which have been implicated in the aggregation of RBPs such as TDP-43 and contribute to the pathogenesis of FTD and ALS (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2013.

claim: Expressing sense (G4C2) repeats can activate the PKR/eIF2a pathway.
source: Previous studies have shown that expressing sense (G4C2) repeats can activate the PKR/eIF2a pathway (Zu et al., 2020) and induce stress granules (Green et al., 2017), which is replicated in our study (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and replicated in the current study.

claim: Expressing sense (G4C2) repeats can induce stress granules.
source: Previous studies have shown that expressing sense (G4C2) repeats can activate the PKR/eIF2a pathway (Zu et al., 2020) and induce stress granules (Green et al., 2017), which is replicated in our study (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and replicated in the current study.

claim: The RAN translation of DPR proteins is increased explicitly by the integrated stress response via eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: It has been suggested the RAN translation of DPR proteins is increased explicitly by the integrated stress response via eIF2α phosphorylation (Cheng et al., 2018; Green et al., 2017) and several DPR proteins such as GR, PR, and GA are toxic (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Choi et al., 2019; Freibaum et al., 2015; Hao et al., 2019; Kanekura et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016; May et al., 2014; Mizielinska et al., 2014; Schludi et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2015; Wen et al., 2014; Yamakawa et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2014; Zu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing ISR-mediated increase in RAN translation.

claim: Several DPR proteins such as GR, PR, and GA are toxic.
source: It has been suggested the RAN translation of DPR proteins is increased explicitly by the integrated stress response via eIF2α phosphorylation (Cheng et al., 2018; Green et al., 2017) and several DPR proteins such as GR, PR, and GA are toxic (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Choi et al., 2019; Freibaum et al., 2015; Hao et al., 2019; Kanekura et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016; May et al., 2014; Mizielinska et al., 2014; Schludi et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2015; Wen et al., 2014; Yamakawa et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2014; Zu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to studies showing DPR protein toxicity.

claim: Activation of PKR/eIF2α by C9ORF72 antisense repeat expanded RNAs may lead to additional accumulation of DPR proteins and toxicity.
source: Thus, activation of PKR/eIF2α by C9ORF72 antisense repeat expanded RNAs may lead to additional accumulation of DPR proteins and toxicity.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential consequences of PKR/eIF2α activation.

claim: ASOs specifically targeting C9ORF72 sense G4C2 repeat expanded RNAs showed great promise in a preclinical mouse model expressing 450 G4C2 repeats.
source: Our previous work with ASOs specifically targeting C9ORF72 sense G4C2 repeat expanded RNAs showed great promise in a preclinical mouse model expressing 450 G4C2 repeats (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: There was a recent setback in a clinical trial using ASOs to treat C9ALS patients.
source: Unfortunately, there was a recent setback in a clinical trial using these ASOs to treat C9ALS patients (Mar 2022, news release by Biogen Inc).
evidence: This is a factual statement about a clinical trial outcome.

claim: Metformin inhibits PKR activation, reduces DPR proteins RAN translated from the sense strand, and improves behavioral and pathological deficits in BAC transgenic mice expressing G4C2 repeats.
source: On this note, Zu et al. recently showed that metformin, an FDA-approved drug widely used for treating type 2 diabetes, inhibits PKR activation, reduces DPR proteins RAN translated from the sense strand, and improves behavioral and pathological deficits in BAC transgenic mice expressing G4C2 repeats (Zu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zu et al., 2020.

claim: The activation of PKR in BAC transgenic mice and in C9ORF72 patients might result from the antisense repeat expanded RNAs.
source: Our study now suggests that the activation of PKR in these BAC transgenic mice and in C9ORF72 patients might result from the antisense repeat expanded RNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the current study.

claim: PKR is constitutively and ubiquitously expressed in vertebrate cells including zebrafish.
source: It is interesting to note that PKR, constitutively and ubiquitously expressed in vertebrate cells including zebrafish, is not found in plants, fungi, protists, or invertebrates such as Drosophila (Martinez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKR expression, supported by citation.

claim: PKR is not found in plants, fungi, protists, or invertebrates such as Drosophila.
source: It is interesting to note that PKR, constitutively and ubiquitously expressed in vertebrate cells including zebrafish, is not found in plants, fungi, protists, or invertebrates such as Drosophila (Martinez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKR expression, supported by citation.

claim: The absence of PKR in Drosophila may partially explain the difference in toxicities caused by the antisense C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs in Drosophila, zebrafish, and primary neurons.
source: This may partially explain the difference in toxicities caused by the antisense C4G2 repeat expanded RNAs in Drosophila, zebrafish, and primary neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation about why antisense RNAs are not toxic in Drosophila but are toxic in vertebrate models.

claim: Patients with more antisense RNA foci tend to have an earlier age of symptom onset.
source: Mizielinska et al., 2013 showed that patients with more antisense RNA foci tend to have an earlier age of symptom onset and, more intriguingly, antisense RNA foci are shown to be associated with nucleoli and mislocalization of TDP-43 in two different studies (Aladesuyi Arogundade et al., 2019; Cooper-Knock et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mizielinska et al., 2013.

claim: Antisense RNA foci are shown to be associated with nucleoli and mislocalization of TDP-43.
source: Mizielinska et al., 2013 showed that patients with more antisense RNA foci tend to have an earlier age of symptom onset and, more intriguingly, antisense RNA foci are shown to be associated with nucleoli and mislocalization of TDP-43 in two different studies (Aladesuyi Arogundade et al., 2019; Cooper-Knock et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aladesuyi Arogundade et al., 2019 and Cooper-Knock et al., 2015.
